paragraphs.heading: A weak layer under the plates
paragraphs.text: The asthenosphere is a soft, ductile zone in Earth's upper mantle. Its name comes from Ancient Greek and means 'without strength'. It sits beneath the lithosphere, the stiff outer shell of the planet, starting somewhere between about 80 and 200 km down. It reaches as deep as roughly 700 km, though its bottom edge is not sharply defined.

paragraphs.heading: Almost solid, but able to flow
paragraphs.text: This layer is not a sea of molten rock. It is made of peridotite, a rock built mostly from the minerals olivine and pyroxene, and it is almost entirely solid. Only a tiny share of the rock, under 0.1%, is melted, and that small amount helps make it weak. Here the mantle rock comes closer to its melting point than anywhere else, and the heat and pressure there let it deform at rates measured in centimetres per year.

paragraphs.heading: Why the plates can move
paragraphs.text: Nearer the surface, where it is cooler, mantle rock acts stiffly; deeper and hotter, it deforms like soft putty. The boundary between the two is usually placed where the temperature reaches 1,300 °C. The rigid plates above are thought to float on the slowly flowing asthenosphere and slide about on its upper part. That arrangement is what allows tectonic plates to move, and it makes a balance called isostatic equilibrium possible.

paragraphs.heading: Found by listening to quakes
paragraphs.text: Seismic waves travel more slowly through the asthenosphere than through the mantle above it, so it has been called the low-velocity zone. Finding that slow zone told seismologists the weak layer existed, because these waves slow down when rock is less rigid. A little melt could explain the slowdown. But the layer still carries S waves, so it cannot be fully molten.

paragraphs.heading: An unsolved puzzle
paragraphs.text: Exactly what makes the layer so weak is not fully settled. Partial melting is the usual answer, yet 0.1% melt seems too little to explain it fully. Other ideas include grains of rock sliding slightly past one another, eased by traces of water and carbon dioxide. Under ocean plates, the motion of the plates may itself help weaken the rock below.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's main magma source
paragraphs.text: Where asthenosphere rock creeps upward, it undergoes much more decompression melting, which makes it the planet's leading source of magma. Most of that magma erupts at mid-ocean ridges and becomes mid-ocean ridge basalt, the rock of the ocean crust. Upwelling asthenosphere also feeds some magmas above subduction zones and in regions of continental rifting.
